title: Mahinda to Sri Lanka
hook: Ashoka's son Mahinda brings the teaching to the island (Mahavamsa 14)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moggaliputta Tissa at the council in Pataliputta, as the Theravada chronicles tell it. Your line was the chronicles remember. Did you hear someone remember a story differently? Today, the end of the week, and a journey. Day eight hundred sixty-one.

A king is hunting on a mountain. He's chasing a deer through the trees, bow in hand, his men somewhere behind him. Then a voice calls him by name. He turns, and standing on the rock above him is a monk in robes, calm, unarmed, waiting. The king is Devanampiya Tissa, ruler of the island of Lanka. The monk, the Mahavamsa says, is Mahinda, son of the emperor Ashoka. The deer is gone. The conversation is about to begin.
screen: `A KING HUNTING A DEER.` → `A VOICE CALLS HIS NAME.` → `A MONK ON THE ROCK.`

segments.voice: First, the test. Before he teaches anything, Mahinda checks whether the king can think. He points to a tree. What is this called? A mango, says the king. Are there other mangoes besides this one? Many. And besides this mango and the other mangoes, are there other trees? Many, but they aren't mangoes. And besides the other mangoes and the trees that aren't mangoes, is there another? Yes, says the king: this mango tree. Then Mahinda asks the same about relatives, and the king answers: besides my kin and those who aren't my kin, there's myself. The chronicle says Mahinda saw then that the king was sharp, and ready. Second, the teaching. Mahinda preaches a discourse to the king and his men there on the mountain, and the king, the chronicle says, takes refuge with the people around him. Third, a son of an emperor. In the chronicle's telling, Mahinda had left a prince's life to become a monk, and he was sent out after the council at Pataliputta. Tradition says Ashoka's own children carried the teaching to the island. However historians weigh the chronicle, in its telling this meeting is where the island's Buddhist story begins. Fourth, the week behind us. We started with a split, the Sthaviras and the Mahasanghikas, and accounts that differ. Then eighteen schools and many readings. Then Ashoka's remorse, carved in stone. His edicts asking respect for every faith. Wells, medicine and shade. A council the chronicles remember. And now a monk on a rock, and a teaching that has crossed the sea.
screen: `THE MANGO RIDDLE.` · `A TEACHING ON THE MOUNTAIN.` · `A SON OF ASHOKA.` · `THIS WEEK: FROM SPLIT TO SEA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recall who brought it to you. Settle, and breathe. Think back to how whatever you hold most deeply first reached you. A faith, a practice, a way of being kind, a love of quiet. Who carried it to your door? A grandparent, a teacher, a friend, a stranger, a book someone left lying around. Let one face come to mind. Remember the moment if you can. Hold them with gratitude for a few breaths, whether they're near, far, or gone. The bell holds the time.
Mahinda. Ashoka's son who met the island's king on a mountain and tested him with a riddle about a mango tree. Today's word.
Your line: the teaching crossed the sea. Today, send a short thank-you to the person who first brought you something you treasure, or say their name with gratitude. Day eight hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Sri Lankan Buddhists remember Mahinda's arrival each year at the Poson full moon, when pilgrims climb the hill of Mihintale, where tradition places the meeting with the king.

what it means: in the chronicle, Ashoka's son meets the island's king on a mountain, tests him with a riddle, and teaches him.

what a scholar hears: the account comes from the Mahavamsa, a chronicle kept by Sri Lankan monks; historians weigh its miracles and details carefully, while the meeting stands at the start of the island's Buddhist story as the chronicle tells it.

notes: Confirm the mango riddle and the kinsmen riddle in Mahavamsa 14, and the order of questions.
The chronicle has Mahinda arrive through the air; the script leaves this out and says 'standing on the rock'. Confirm that the omission is acceptable.
The discourse preached is the Culahatthipadopama Sutta (MN 27) in the chronicle; the script says only 'a discourse'.
Week-end look-back covers days 855–861. Day 855's carry 'accounts differ' is echoed.
